name: Mummy Brown
poem: A brown ground, quite literally, from ground Egyptian mummies — a pigment painters used for centuries before learning what it was.

recipe.note: A muted earth brown — warm red and ochre quieted with black.

lenses.label: Art History
lenses.intro: For three centuries painters reached for a tube of brown without asking too hard where it came from — and the answer turned out to be: people.

entries.title: Liberty Leading the People
entries.blurb: The warm browns of Liberty's exposed torso are very likely mummy brown — Delacroix bought it by the tube from Paris colourmen without much curiosity.

entries.title: Pre-Raphaelite Landscapes
entries.blurb: The Pre-Raphaelites used mummy brown for shadows in flesh and rich earth tones — until Burne-Jones discovered the source and held a funeral for his last tube.

entries.title: Studio of Martin Drolling
entries.blurb: The French painter ground entire Egyptian mummies for pigment — including, by some accounts, the royal mummies of Persian kings. A barrel kept under the easel.

lenses.label: Fashion
lenses.intro: Mummy brown is the colour Victorian respectability dressed in — earnest, modest, just gloomy enough.

entries.title: Victorian Mourning Dress
entries.blurb: After the first year of pure black, Victorian widows transitioned through brown, grey and mauve — mummy brown was a popular intermediate shade.

entries.title: Edwardian Walking Suits
entries.blurb: A muted brown tweed walking suit was the ultimate sensible daywear — country enough to be practical, dark enough to be appropriate at any hour.

entries.title: Trench Coats
entries.blurb: The original trench coat was developed in earth-brown gabardine for British officers — a colour that would blend with mud and not betray its wearer.

lenses.label: Nature
lenses.intro: Brown is what the world tends toward — leaves, blood, soil, time. Mummy brown is just that arc accelerated.

entries.title: Egyptian Desert
entries.blurb: The colour of the desert that preserved every mummy ever ground for paint — a dry brown that has held human bodies intact for four thousand years.

entries.title: Peat Bog Bodies
entries.blurb: Bog acids tan corpses to the exact brown of the bog itself — Tollund Man, Lindow Man, the Yde Girl: each a perfect mummy in different chemistry.

entries.title: Bitumen Seeps
entries.blurb: Naturally occurring asphalt — the same bitumen Egyptian embalmers may have used, and the same chemistry that preserves Pleistocene mammoths in California.

lenses.label: Pop Culture
lenses.intro: The pigment's macabre history makes it one of the most-cited examples of art's quietly unethical sourcing.

entries.title: Burne-Jones's Funeral
entries.blurb: When the Pre-Raphaelite painter learned what was actually in his tube of mummy brown, he buried the paint in his garden — with a small ceremony.

entries.title: The Last Tubes
entries.blurb: The London colour merchants admitted to a journalist that they'd run out of mummies — and quietly stopped selling the colour after over a century.

entries.title: "It's Just Brown"
entries.blurb: Many paintings catalogued as containing mummy brown are now believed to contain ordinary umber — colourmen substituted freely as supply dwindled.

lenses.label: Etymology
lenses.intro: The colour's name is also its recipe — a rare honest pigment, even when its history was not.

entries.title: "Mumia"
entries.blurb: The Persian word for the black, waxy embalming substance — Europeans assumed it was the source of every mummy's preservation, and ate it as medicine.

entries.title: "Caput Mortuum"
entries.blurb: An alchemical synonym — the dark brown residue left after distillation, named for its colour and its grim resemblance to the inside of a skull.

entries.title: "Egyptian Brown"
entries.blurb: When "mummy" became too uncomfortable to print on tube labels, late-Victorian colourmen rebranded the same pigment as the more polite "Egyptian Brown."

lenses.label: Symbolism
lenses.intro: The colour holds the strangest possible weight — beauty and necropolis at once, ordinary by sight, indefensible by source.

entries.title: The Material of Time
entries.blurb: Mummy brown is literal memento mori — every brushstroke on a Victorian canvas was, sometimes, a brushstroke of someone dead for three thousand years.

entries.title: Egyptomania
entries.blurb: After Napoleon's Egyptian campaign, mummies became fashionable salon entertainment — unwrapping parties were attended like operas, and the leftover bodies went to colourmen.

entries.title: The Ethics of the Tube
entries.blurb: Mummy brown is the most-cited example in every conversation about art and provenance — a reminder that beautiful things sometimes have unbearable sources.
